title: Physical and Chemical Changes
seo_title: Grade 5 Science: Physical and Chemical Changes Worksheets (Ontario Curriculum)
standard_text: Distinguish between physical changes and chemical changes; identify signs of chemical change; assess the effects of changes in matter on the environment and ways to reduce harm. (summary of the Ontario Science and Technology curriculum, 2022, Strand C: Matter and Energy – Properties of and Changes in Matter)
meta_desc: Free Grade 5 science worksheets on physical and chemical changes, signs of a chemical change, reversible and irreversible changes. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: A chemical change makes a new substance.
key_sub: Physical changes (melting, cutting, dissolving) can often be reversed; chemical changes usually cannot.
body_html:
How to think about it

In a physical change, the substance stays the same. In a chemical change, a new substance forms.

  • Physical changes: melting, freezing, cutting, crushing, dissolving.
  • Chemical changes: burning, rusting, cooking, rotting.
  • Signs of a chemical change: gas bubbles, a new colour or smell, light or heat given off, a solid forming.
Example

Is burning toast physical or chemical?

new black substance

cannot change back

Answer: chemical

Example

Is dissolving salt in water physical or chemical?

evaporate the water to get the salt back

Answer: physical

Common mistakes

  • Thinking every change of colour is a chemical change.
  • Thinking dissolving makes the substance disappear.
  • Thinking chemical changes are always dangerous.

faq.q: How can you tell a chemical change happened?
faq.a: Look for a new substance: bubbles of gas, a new colour or smell, light or heat, or a solid forming in a liquid.
No. Melting changes the state, but the substance is still the same.

faq.q: Why do chemical changes matter for the environment?
faq.a: Burning fuels and some factory processes make pollution, so waste must be treated and reduced.

items.e: A candle wick burning makes a new substance with new properties, so it is a chemical change.

items.q: Why do scientists repeat an investigation several times?
c: to check that the results are reliable

No, a new substance always forms.
items.e: Not every chemical change is easy to see. More tests (like testing with a magnet or heating) can give more evidence.

items.q: Ella says, 'Cooking an egg is reversible because the egg is still there.' Why is she wrong?

items.q: Leah drops the same size antacid tablet into cold water and hot water. Which variable is she testing?

items.q: A sealed bag holds 50 g of vinegar and a small cup with 15 g of baking soda. The bag is tipped so they mix and the bag puffs up. What is the total mass now?
items.e: A new gas forms, but the bag is sealed, so nothing gets out: 50 + 15 = 65 g. The particles are rearranged, not destroyed.

items.q: A sealed bag holds 120 g of vinegar and a small cup with 10 g of baking soda. The bag is tipped so they mix and the bag puffs up. What is the total mass now?
items.e: A new gas forms, but the bag is sealed, so nothing gets out: 120 + 10 = 130 g. The particles are rearranged, not destroyed.
